name: Ortholux I and Ortholux II

specs.Museum examples: Ortholux I dated 1958 and Ortholux II dated 1975 (Utrecht BIC museum); Ortholux with Ultropak incident-light illuminator, 1961
specs.Catalogue: 1958 Leitz sales catalogue for the ORTHOLUX II research microscope (Deutsches Museum archive)

summary: Leitz's large research microscope stand, made in at least two generations. Examples are held by the Utrecht University microscopy museum and the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh.

name: Ultraphot II

specs.Illumination: 100 W incandescent plus Osram 200 W mercury arc (Luminars system)
specs.Cameras: 35 mm camera head and 4x5 inch camera head with Polaroid film holder
specs.Stand: Matching all-metal work desk with power supply control

summary: A desk-mounted photomicrography system with built-in large-format and 35 mm cameras and both incandescent and mercury-arc illumination.

sources.title: Molecular Expressions museum: Carl Zeiss Ultraphot II

name: Model M inverted microscope

specs.Illumination: Episcopic illuminator in the base and diascopic illuminator above the stage
specs.Options: Phase contrast, interference contrast, photomicrography, cinemicrography, transparent incubator

summary: An inverted microscope for both biological (transmitted) and metallurgical (reflected) work, with accessories for time-lapse cinemicrography of tissue culture.

sources.title: Molecular Expressions museum: Nikon Model M inverted microscope

name: Vanox

specs.Era: Flagship of the Olympus America line during most of the 1970s
specs.Illumination: Tungsten-halogen lamp in the rear base

summary: Olympus research microscope of the 1970s with built-in halogen illumination and an advanced photomicrography system.

name: Universal microscope

specs.Era: One of the premier microscopes of the 1960s
specs.Illumination: Tungsten-halogen lamp for transmitted light; mercury arc for fluorescence and reflected light

summary: A general-purpose research stand for routine and critical microscopy, with transmitted halogen illumination and a mercury lamp for epi-fluorescence.

sources.title: Molecular Expressions museum: Carl Zeiss Universal microscope

name: Inverted "Chemists Microscope"

specs.Designed: 1950s; discontinued in the early to mid 1970s
specs.Illumination: Lamphouse and condenser on a chrome pillar, from above
specs.Focus: Rack and pinion moving the stage

summary: A low-power inverted microscope intended for watching chemical reactions in flasks, which became a common workhorse for checking cell growth in tissue-culture vessels.

sources.title: Molecular Expressions museum: Leitz inverted Chemists Microscope

name: Provis AX70

specs.Control: Multi-control box for observation and photomicrography; data memory cards
specs.Camera ports: 3-way camera light path with data imprinting

summary: Olympus research microscope introduced in 1998 with infinity-corrected optics, apochromatic objectives of higher numerical aperture and integrated photomicrography control.

sources.title: Molecular Expressions museum: Olympus Provis AX70

name: Elmiskop 51
summary: A simple transmission electron microscope using permanent-magnet lenses. The Science Museum Group holds a 1969 example with four boxes of components.

name: EM6B
summary: British transmission electron microscope, model introduced in 1964 according to the Science Museum Group, which holds an example from Thames Polytechnic.

name: EM 75
summary: Dutch transmission electron microscope of about 1957. The Science Museum Group example was used at the Manchester Medical School.

sources.title: Science Museum Group: Philips EM 75 electron microscope (Y1984.261)

name: EMU-2B
summary: American transmission electron microscope from 1946. The Science Museum Group example, from the Animal Virus Research Institute, is displayed as used for examining cultured clinical samples to identify the cause of illness.

name: EM2
summary: British transmission electron microscope made in Manchester; the Science Museum Group holds a 1946 example with its separate control panel.

summary: Scanning electron microscope model from Cambridge Scientific Instruments. The Science Museum Group record is a dummy model and gives conflicting dates (made 1971-1974 versus 1978-1980 in the title).
